newsitem.title: UK: TENNIS-BOOM BATTLE SUSPENDED IN WIMBLEDON GLOOM.
newsitem.headline: TENNIS-BOOM BATTLE SUSPENDED IN WIMBLEDON GLOOM.

text.p: A booming battle between the two fastest servers yet recorded in tennis was suspended in the Wimbledon gloom on Monday with Greg Rusedski looking for the first upset of the championships.
The unseeded 23-year-old was likely to enjoy the more peaceful night's sleep after going 7-6 7-6 and 3-1 up against seventh-seeded Australian Mark Philippoussis.

Rusedski, buoyed by vociferous support from the Centre Court crowd, had held his nerve and his serve against the 20-year-old Philippoussis, who holds the record for the fastest monitored serve at 229 kph.
The Canadian-born Briton, whose own serve has hit more than 225 kph, looked impenetrable and it was not until the ninth game that Philippoussis earned a point against his serve.

Philippoussis, ranked 13th in the world to Rusedski's 27, looked fragile, made several volleying errors and struggled to save four break points and three set points, before putting a volley wide to hand Rusedski the first set tie-break 8-6.
The second set also went entirely with serve and the young Australian had his best chance with four set points at 6-2 in the tie-break.

But as night fell his nerve broke. He misjudged and left a Rusedski return which bounced well within the court to surrender the first point. He then returned to the net and wide on Rusedski's two serves.
But serving again for the set he double faulted twice and then put a forehand into the net for another 8-6 scoreline.
A double fault at 2-1 down in the third set put Rusedski in total command.
Both men came to the match well-prepared for grass -- Philippoussis had beaten Goran Ivanisevic to win at Queen's eight days ago and Rusedski won the Nottingham grass court tournament on Sunday.
But on the lush Wimbledon grass, slippery despite the covers to protect it from recent torrential rain, it was Rusedski who showed the greater touch and determination.

On number one court the match between former Wimbledon champion Michael Stich of Germany and former French and Australian Open champion Jim Courier of the United States was also suspended after both men slipped and slid into the dusk.
Stich was leading 7-6 1-2 when the referee called them off to prevent further falls on the treacherous surface.
Play on Wimbledon's first day was interrupted four times for rain and forecasters predict more to come this week.
But several matches did cough and splutter to completion.
Richard Krajicek dodged the rain showers to begin the defence of his Wimbledon title with a straight-sets win over German Marcello Craca.

Krajicek had only just set foot on court when rain, which teased the organisers throughout the first day of the championships, sent him back to the locker room. Another downpour interrupted his Centre Court match for 75 minutes in the third set but the fourth-seeded Dutchman shrugged off the delays, winning 7-6 6-2 6-4 after one hour 41 minutes of play.
Krajicek, who won the first-set tiebreak 7-5 and then raced to a 4-0 lead in the second set, admitted the match had not been a classic.

"These are the kind of matches that you just have to win and you don't look for beauty," he said. "I felt pretty pressured as defending champion and I felt a little bit nervous but it was a great feeling to get through this match."
Second seed Ivanisevic sped through his first match so fast on Court Two that he had no need to worry about the weather.
Ivanisevic beat Romanian Dinu Pescariu, ranked 106th in the world, 6-1 6-3 6-3 in just 64 minutes.

Tim Henman, who last year inflamed British hopes of the first home winner in the men's singles since 1936 when he reached the quarter-finals, ignited another spark when he defeated Canadian Daniel Nestor 7-6 (13-11) 6-1 6-4 in his opening match.
To Henman fell the honour of baptising the new 11,000-seat Court One which was officially opened with a parade of former champions including Rod Laver, Margaret Court and Martina Navratilova.

Women's fourth seed Iva Majoli, the French Open champion but still a novice on grass, was relieved to get her first win at Wimbledon in three attempts. The Croat beat Argentina's Mariana Diaz Oliva 2-6 6-0 6-3.
"When I won this match I was almost as happy as when I won the French Open," said Majoli. "It was like a release."

There were first-round wins too for fifth seeded American Lindsay Davenport, who beat compatriot Tami Jones 5-7 6-2 6-2 and number 12 Irina Spirlea of Romania, who thrashed Slovak Henrieta Nagyova 6-1 6-0.
